newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan drug makers poised to sell ulcer drugs.
newsitem.headline: Japan drug makers poised to sell ulcer drugs.

text.p: Major Japanese pharmaceutical companies are poised to introduce over-the-counter stomach ulcer drugs, a move the government hopes will help curb surging medical costs.
Drug makers such as Yamanouchi Pharmaceutical Co Ltd, Taisho Pharmaceutical Co Ltd and Fujisawa Pharmaceutical Co Ltd are preparing to launch the drugs in Japan later this year.
The drugs are versions of prescription drugs which are now available only through hospitals.
Analysts said that the market for such drugs may grow considerably as consumers will be able to buy the stronger drugs without obtaining a doctor's prescription.
But some analysts were sceptical about whether there was a large market for the drugs, saying people will likely continue to want to receive treatment in hospitals.

Ryoichi Urushihara, analyst at Nomura Securities Financial Research Centre, said that Yamanouchi, Taisho and Takeda Chemical Industries Ltd will benefit from the introduction of the new non-prescription ulcer drugs.
"The three companies will likely each see sales for their ulcer drugs exceed 10 billion yen after five years," said Urushihara.
Yamanouchi said last week it plans to launch an over-the-counter version of its ulcer-fighting drug Gastar after it obtains government approval.

A company spokesman said sales of the new drug are likely to start before end of this year, and will help the company reach expected parent sales of 320 billion yen ($2.83 billion) in the current business year to March 1998, up from 312 billion yen ($2.76 billion) in 1996/97.
Some Japanese pharmaceutical firms have teamed up with major overseas drug makers to enter the market.
Taisho plans to introduce the ulcer drug Zantac, developed by Glaxo Wellcome Plc, later this year.
"Our foreign partner was attracted to us because of our strong marketing network for over-the-counter drugs," a company spokesman said.
Fujisawa is preparing to launch SmithKline Beecham Plc's non-prescription digestive drug Tagamet in Japan.
The company may also develop a version of its prescription anti-allergy medicine for the over-the-counter market, a spokesman said.
"We hope to expand our product line as we expect that the need to cut medical expenses will promote growth of the market for non-prescription drugs," he said.

With increased use of over-the-counter drugs, the government hopes to reduce National Health Insurance spending, under which drugs prescribed at hospitals are wholly or partly reimbursed by the government.
But Masatake Miyoshi, an analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan, said the new ulcer-fighting drugs are unlikely to be that profitable as the market's growth will likely be limited.

"About eight drug makers are expected to compete in a fairly small market," he said. "The size of the market for the new drugs will likely reach only about 20 billion yen ($176 million) per year at the most." ($1=113 yen)
